text: -operative chemoradi- otherapy significantly improved the 3-year mortality rates compared with surgery alone, and a later meta-analysis8 found a significant survival benefit for neoadjuvant chem- oradiotherapy (versus surgery alone) in patients with oesophageal adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcino- ma. Pre-operative chemoradiotherapy has thus become a common approach for patients with resectable oesopha- geal cancer.2,4 Meta-analysis8 also suggested some surviv- al benefit of neoadjuvant chemotherapy without radiother- apy in those with adenocarcinoma, but not for those with squamous cell carcinoma. A systematic review9 found that pre-operative chemotherapy may offer a survival advan- tage compared with surgery alone, although the evidence was considered to be inconclusive. However, some do not recommend the use of chemotherapy, either pre- or post- operatively, as standard of care.2 In half to two-thirds of patients the disease is too advanced at presentation for anything but palliation. Those with poor performance status should be offered supportive care.2 This may include brachytherapy, laser therapy, stent place- ment, or photodynamic therapy with photosensitisers such as porfimer sodium to relieve obstruction.2 Brachytherapy may be a better primary therapy for obstruction than a stent.10 In those patients with good performance status, chemotherapy may also offer some palliation of the dis- ease. Standard options include cisplatin-based, fluoropyri- midine-based, irinotecan-based, oxaliplatin-based or tax- ane-based combinations.2,5,11 Chemoradiotherapy may also be used.5 1.
